lead: At the boundary between two transparent media, one light wave becomes two: a reflected wave returns into the first medium, and a refracted wave enters the second with a changed direction and speed. The split is controlled by the refractive indices. The idea lets you design mirrors, lenses, optical fibres, anti-reflection coatings and every thin-film device in this unit. It also fixes the phase bookkeeping that later interference chapters depend on. This chapter states the laws, gives the normal-incidence reflectance formula, and explains the π phase change on reflection from a denser medium.
prereq: You need: Unit 3, electromagnetic waves and uniform plane waves; light is an electromagnetic wave whose electric field oscillates perpendicular to its direction of travel.

sections.h3: Wavefronts, rays, and the two laws

blocks.text: Light travels as a wave. A wavefront is a surface on which the electric field has the same phase. A ray is a line drawn perpendicular to the wavefront; it shows the direction in which energy travels. In a uniform medium the rays are straight. At a flat boundary the incident ray, the reflected ray, the refracted ray and the normal all lie in one plane. The normal is the line perpendicular to the boundary at the point where the ray strikes.

Huygens' construction treats every point on a wavefront as a source of small secondary wavelets; the new wavefront is their envelope. One line is enough here: it explains why a plane wave stays plane and why the ray bends when the speed changes. The laws follow.
Law of reflection: the angle of incidence i equals the angle of reflection r′. Both angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface. Law of refraction is Snell's law.
n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r
blocks.where: n₁ is the refractive index of the first medium; n₂ is the refractive index of the second medium; i is the angle of incidence in medium 1, measured from the normal; r is the angle of refraction in medium 2, measured from the normal.

blocks.text: When n₂ > n₁, r < i: the ray bends toward the normal. When n₂ < n₁, it bends away. Some syllabi call this reflection and refraction of EM waves.

sections.h3: Refractive index, speed, and total internal reflection

blocks.text: The refractive index n of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed in the medium. Because v ≤ c, n ≥ 1. Air is close to n = 1.00; water is about 1.33; ordinary glass is about 1.50. The frequency stays the same when light crosses a boundary. The speed and wavelength change.

blocks.where: n is the refractive index, a pure number; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light in vacuum; v is the speed of light in the medium, in m/s.

blocks.text: The wavelength in the second medium is λ₂ = λ₁ (n₁/n₂), where λ₁ and λ₂ are the wavelengths in medium 1 and medium 2. This changed speed is what bends the wavefront and therefore the ray.

Total internal reflection occurs when light tries to go from a denser medium (higher n) to a rarer medium (lower n). At the critical angle C, the refracted ray grazes the boundary at 90°. Snell's law gives n₁ sin C = n₂ sin 90° = n₂.

blocks.where: C is the critical angle measured from the normal; n₁ is the index of the denser medium the light starts in; n₂ is the index of the rarer medium. For a medium of index n against air, n₂ = 1 and sin C = 1/n.

blocks.text: If i > C, no refracted ray enters the second medium; all the light is reflected back. This is the idea behind optical fibres, where light is trapped inside a core of higher index surrounded by cladding of lower index (see Unit 5, Fibre Optics).

sections.h3: How much reflects at normal incidence

blocks.text: At normal incidence the ray strikes along the normal, so i = 0° and r = 0°. The boundary still splits the wave. For a transparent boundary with no absorption, the reflectance R is the fraction of power reflected, and the transmittance T is the fraction transmitted.

blocks.where: n₁ is the index of the medium the light comes from; n₂ is the index of the medium it enters; R is a pure number between 0 and 1; T is also a pure number.

blocks.text: For air to glass, n₁ = 1.00 and n₂ = 1.50, R = 0.04 and T = 0.96: 4% reflects, 96% enters. For glass to air the square is the same, so R is still 0.04 at normal incidence. A larger index jump reflects more.

There is a phase rule at reflection. When light reflects from a medium of higher refractive index (denser medium, n₂ > n₁), the reflected electric field changes sign. A sign change is a phase change of π radians, equivalent to half a wavelength. When light reflects from a lower-index medium (rarer medium, n₂ < n₁), there is no such phase change. This π shift is the reason a thin film can cancel reflection; it enters every thin-film calculation in 4.2 and 4.5.
At oblique incidence the reflected fraction depends on polarization. Brewster's angle is the angle at which the reflected light is completely polarized; it is named here and worked out in 4.7.

figure.caption: The incident wave in air (n₁ = 1.00) meets a glass boundary (n₂ = 1.50) at i = 30°. The reflected ray keeps 30°; the refracted ray bends toward the normal to 19.5°, so n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r.

spec.title: One wave at a boundary
spec.aria: A flow from the incident wave in air to the glass boundary, where it splits into a reflected wave going back at 30° and a refracted wave bending into the glass at 19.5°.

examples.question: A ray of light in air (n₁ = 1.00) strikes a flat glass surface (n₂ = 1.50) at an angle of 30.0° to the normal. (a) Find the angle of refraction. (b) Find the reflectance and transmittance at normal incidence for the same air-glass boundary.
steps: Use Snell's law: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r.
Find r = sin⁻¹(0.3333) = 19.5°. The ray bends toward the normal because n₂ > n₁.
examples.check:
import math
n1 = 1.00
n2 = 1.50
i = 30.0
r = math.degrees(math.asin((n1/n2)*math.sin(math.radians(i))))
R = ((n1 - n2)/(n1 + n2))**2
T = 1 - R
print(round(r, 1))
print(round(R, 2))
print(round(T, 2))

traps: Angles of incidence, reflection and refraction are always measured from the normal. Measuring from the glass surface gives wrong numbers and is the most common slip.
The formula R = ((n₁ − n₂)/(n₁ + n₂))² is for normal incidence only. At an angle, the reflected fraction also depends on polarization.
The π phase change happens only when light reflects from a denser medium (higher n). Reflection from a rarer medium has no π change.
T = 1 − R assumes a transparent boundary with no absorption. A real glass surface may absorb or scatter some light.
Total internal reflection needs light going from higher n to lower n. It cannot happen from air to glass, whatever the angle.

quiz.q: State the law of reflection. From where are the angles measured?
quiz.a: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane. Angles are measured from the normal.

quiz.q: Why does a ray bend toward the normal when it enters glass from air?
quiz.a: Glass has a higher refractive index, so light travels slower in glass. The wavefront spacing changes and Snell's law gives n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r with n₂ > n₁, so r < i.

quiz.q: Light in air (n₁ = 1.00) hits water (n₂ = 1.33) at 40.0° to the normal. Find the angle of refraction.
Light in glass (n = 1.50) goes toward air. Find the critical angle and state what happens at 45°.
quiz.a: sin C = 1/1.50 = 0.667, so C = 41.8°. At 45°, which is greater than C, total internal reflection occurs and no light refracts into air.

quiz.q: Find R and T at normal incidence for air to diamond (n = 2.42).
Why is there a π phase change when light reflects from a denser medium?
quiz.a: The boundary conditions force the reflected electric field to change sign when n₂ > n₁. A sign change is a phase shift of π radians, equal to half a wavelength.

quiz.q: For air to glass, does the reflected wave get a π phase change? What about glass to air?
quiz.a: Air to glass: yes, because glass is denser. Glass to air: no, because air is rarer. This difference controls thin-film interference.

beyond: Not for the exam. The full Fresnel equations give reflection and transmission at any angle and for each polarization; they reduce to the normal-incidence formulas here. Total internal reflection also creates an evanescent wave that leaks a short distance into the rarer medium, used in fibre sensors and microscope techniques. Thin-film design software stacks many such boundaries to make filters, mirrors and anti-reflection coatings. Metamaterials and photonic crystals engineer n to control reflection in unusual ways. Search next for Fresnel equations, evanescent wave, and thin-film transfer matrix.
